                                                 Finite groups and rings generating varieties of rapid growth
                                                                                     Alexander Olshanskii


                                                                                             Abstract
                                                     Let A be a finite universal algebra. Then the cardinalities of the n-generated free algebras Fn
                                                                                                                                                   n
                                                 in the variety (equational class) generated byp A satisfy G. Birkhoff’s inequality: |Fn | ≤ |A||A|
                                                 for n = 1, 2, . . . It follows that lim supn→∞ n log |Fn | ≤ |A|. When A is a finite group or a
                                                 finite nonassociative algebra, we obtain a criterion for equality in this estimate; equivalently, a
                                                 criterion for maximal growth of the sequence {|Fn |}∞ n=1 .
arXiv:2606.04577v3 [math.GR] 31 Jul 2026




                                               Key words: finite groups, finite rings, varieties of groups and rings.
                                               AMS Mathematical Subject Classification: 20E10, 20D99, 17A30, 08B20.


                                           1    Introduction
                                           Let A be a finite algebra of a fixed signature. The variety of algebras var A generated by A consists
                                           of all algebras of the same signature satisfying every identity that holds in A. A basic theorem of
                                           G. Birkhoff [3, 5] says that var A is the smallest class of algebras containing A and closed under
                                           taking subalgebras, homomorphic images, and Cartesian products.
                                               The cardinality of every n-generated algebra in the variety var A is bounded by the cardinality of
                                           the n-generated free algebra Fn in var A. The algebra Fn isomorphically embeds in a direct power
                                           of the algebra A, and its cardinality is bounded from above by the double-exponential function
                                                 n
                                           |A||A| , where |A|pis the cardinality of the algebra A (see [3] or subsection 0.3 in [5]). It follows
                                           that lim supn→∞ n log |Fn | ≤ |A|. We denote the left-hand side of this inequality by pot A and call
                                           it the potential of the finite algebra A.
                                               For example, if G is a nontrivial finite group, then pot G = 1 if G is nilpotent and pot G ≥ 2
                                           otherwise ([7], 24.52). The same alternative holds for finite-dimensional (non-associative) algebras
                                           over finite fields [1].
                                               As early as 1937, it was noticed by B.H. Neumann [6] that Birkhoff’s estimate can be improved
                                           in many cases. Our goal is to find necessary and sufficient conditions on A under which the potential
                                           pot A attains its maximal possible value, namely conditions equivalent to the equality pot A = |A|,
                                           where A is either a finite group or a finite, not necessarily associative, ring.
                                               Recall that a nontrivial group (ring) A is called monolithic if the intersection of all nontrivial
                                           normal subgroups (2-sided ideals) of A is nontrivial. This intersection is the monolith of the
                                           monolithic group (respectively, ring) A.
                                           Theorem 1. Let G be a finite group. The equality pot G = |G| holds if and only if
                                                (*) G is a monolithic group with a non-abelian monolith.
                                                Moreover, under condition (*), there exist positive constants c1 and c2 such that
                                           c1 |G|n < log |Fn | < c2 |G|n for the n-generated free groups Fn in the variety var G.

                                                                                                 1
2                                                A.Yu. Olshanskii


    Many nonsimple groups satisfy condition (*); for example, the symmetric groups Sn for n ≥ 5
and any wreath product of a non-cyclic finite simple group and a nontrivial finite group.
    A (not necessarily associative) non-zero ring A is a prime ring if the product of any two nonzero
(2-sided) ideals of A is nonzero. The following is an analogue of Theorem 1.

Theorem 2. Let A be a (non-associative) finite ring. The equality pot A = |A| holds if and only
if A is a prime ring.
     Moreover, if A is a prime ring, then there exist positive constants c1 and c2 such that
c1 |A|n < log |Fn | < c2 |A|n for the n-generated free rings Fn in the variety var A.

   Classical results in ring theory imply that every finite prime associative ring is simple ([9],
Section 98). By contrast, the following construction gives a nonsimple prime algebra over a field
with basis (e, f ) and multiplication rules e2 = f , ef = f , f e = 0, and f 2 = f . It has only one
one-dimensional ideal ⟨f ⟩.


2     Sufficiency in Theorem 1
Lemma 1. Let G be a finite monolithic group with a non-abelian monolith. Let H be a direct
product H1 × . . . × Hk with projections πi : H → Hi . Let S be a subdirect product, i.e. a subgroup
of H such that πi (S) = Hi for all i, with an epimorphism ϕ : S → G. Then there exist an index i
and an epimorphism ψ : Hi → G such that ϕ = ψπi .

Proof. By induction on k; this is trivial when k ≤ 1; assume k ≥ 2. The subgroups ϕ(S ∩ Hi ) are
normal and pairwise centralize each other, so at most one of them is nontrivial since the monolith
of G = ϕ(S) is non-abelian. After reindexing, we may assume ϕ(S ∩ Hk ) is trivial. Let π be the
projection S → H1 × . . . × Hk−1 and S ′ = π(S). Then ϕπ −1 is a well-defined epimorphism S ′ → G
since ker π = S ∩ Hk and ϕ(S ∩ Hk ) = {1}. By induction, there exists i < k and an epimorphism
ψ : Hi → G such that ϕπ −1 = ψπi′ , where πi′ is the projection of H1 × . . . × Hk−1 onto Hi . Hence
ϕ = ψπi′ π = ψπi , as required.

Lemma 2. Let G be a finite monolithic group with non-abelian monolith M . Let GI be a finite direct
power of G, with direct factors Gi isomorphic to G for i ∈ I. For a fixed n ≥ 1, let x1 , . . . , xn ∈ GI
and x1i , . . . xni be their projections in Gi . Assume that the elements x1i , . . . xni generate Gi for
i ∈ I and suppose the n-tuples (x1i , . . . xni ), i ∈ I, lie in pairwise distinct (Aut G)-orbits on Gn .
Then the subgroup B of GI generated by x1 , . . . , xn contains M I .

Proof. Arguing by contradiction, assume that B does not contain the copy Mi of the monolith M
for some i ∈ I. Since Mi is the monolith of Gi , it follows that B ∩ Mi = {1}, because the subgroup
B ∩ Mi of the subdirect product B must be normal in the factor Gi . Therefore B ∩ Gi = {1}
since nontrivial
           Q           normal subgroups of Gi contain Mi . Hence B can be subdirectly embedded in the
product j̸=i Gj .
    By Lemma 1, the projection πi : B → Gi factors as ψπj , where j ̸= i and ψ is an isomorphism
Gj → Gi Thus, the n-tuple (x1 , . . . , xn ) is mapped to (x1i , . . . , xni ) under πi and it is mapped
to (x1j , . . . , xnj ) under ψ. It follows that the isomorphism ψ maps (x1j , . . . , xnj ) to (x1i , . . . , xni ),
contrary to the assumption that these n-tuples belong to different Aut G-orbits. The lemma is
proved by contradiction.
                                                                                                     3


    Remark 1. For finite simple, non-abelian groups G, the statement of Lemma 2 has been known
for a long time, see [4].
    For each proper subgroup H ≤ G, we have |H| ≤ |G|/2 and the number of n-tuples of elements
from H is equal to |H|n . If s is the number of proper subgroups of G, then the number of n-tuples
generating G is at least |G|n − s(|G|/2)n = |G|n (1 − O(2−n )). Thus, for some constant c > 0 and
                                              |G|n            −n )) > c|G|n n-tuples lying in pairwise
all sufficiently large n, there are at least |Aut G| (1 − O(2
distinct (Aut G)-orbits. By Lemma 2, there is an n-generated subgroup B = B(n) of order at least
        n
|M |c|G| in some GI . Since B(n) ∈ var G, we obtain log |Fn | ≥ log |B(n)| > c1 |G|n for some c1 > 0
and every n ≥ 1, as required. Birkhoff’s inequality implies log |Fn | < c2 |G|n for some c2 > 0. This
proves the sufficiency part of Theorem 1.


3    Necessity in Theorem 1
Lemma 3. Let G1 and G2 be finite groups. Assume that a finite group G generates the variety
V = var (G1 , G2 ). Then pot G = max(pot G1 , pot G2 ). In particular, if G is not monolithic, then
pot G = pot (G/N ) ≤ |G/N | for a non-trivial normal subgroup N of G.

Proof. Clearly, pot G ≥ max(pot G1 , pot G2 ). On the other hand, the n-generated V-free group Fn
is a subdirect product of the free groups Fn′ and Fn′′ in the varieties var G1 and var G2 ([7], 15.82),
and hence |Fn | ≤ |Fn′ ||Fn′′ |. To estimate pot G from above, it remains only to note that, for any
sequences of positive integers {a′n }∞           ′′ ∞
                                       n=1 and {an }n=1 , we have
                                  p                          p
                          lim sup n log(a′n a′′n ) = lim sup n log a′n + log a′′n
                            n→∞                      n→∞
                                           p                   p
                             = max(lim sup n log a′n , lim sup n log a′′n ).
                                       n→∞                 n→∞

   If the group G is not monolithic, there are two nontrivial normal subgroups N1 and N2 in G
such that N1 ∩ N2 = {1}. Then G is a subdirect product of the factor groups G1 = G/N1 and
G2 = G/N2 , and var G = var {G1 , G2 }. Hence pot G = max(pot G1 , pot G2 ), which completes the
proof.

Lemma 4. Let Q be a group and N be a (right) Q-module. Assume that N = ⊕i Mi is a direct
sum of isomorphic finite Q-submodules Mi of cardinality m. Then any n-generated submodule L of
N has cardinality at most mnm .

Proof. There are module isomorphisms αij : Mi → Mj such that αjk αij = αik for all i, j, k. If
a ∈ Mi and the indices i, i1 , ..., ik are pairwise different, then the ’diagonal-type’ sum
b = a + αii1 (a) + . . . + αiik (a) generates a Q-submodule isomorphic to the submodule generated
by a, and so b generates a submodule of order at most m. Since every element a′ of Mj equals
αij (a) for some a ∈ Mi , any element of N can be decomposed as a sum of at most m ’diagonal’
elements. Hence every one-generated submodule of N has order at most mm , and so |L| ≤ (mm )n ,
as required.

Lemma 5. Let G be a finite group and N an abelian normal subgroup of a group H ∈ var G, on
which the finite group R = H/N acts by conjugation, and N = ⊕i Mi be a direct sum of isomorphic
4                                              A.Yu. Olshanskii


finite R-submodules Mi of cardinality m. Then for every n ≥ 1, any n-generated subgroup S of H
                        log |R|
has order at most |G||G| 2 mnm .

Proof. One can choose at most log2 |R| generators, say x1 , ..., xk , in S whose natural images generate
the subgroup Q = SN/N ≤ R. By multiplying the other n − k generators by some products of
x±1         ±1
  1 , ..., xk , one obtains a set of generators {x1 , ..., xk , yk+1 , . . . yn } in S, where yi ∈ N for i > k.
    Since the subgroup K generated by x1 , ..., xk belongs to var G, the order of K does not exceed
             log |R|
C = |G||G| 2 . The normal closure L of the elements yk+1 , . . . , yn in S is a Q-submodule and so
its cardinality is at most m(n−k)m by Lemma 4. Thus, |S| = |KL| ≤ |K||L| ≤ Cmnm .

    Proposition 1. If M is an abelian normal subgroup of a finite group G, then pot G ≤ |G/M |.

Proof. Recall that the n-generated (var G)-free group Fn is embedded in a direct power GI for
some I. Denote by H the product Fn M I , so H/M I is a subgroup of T I , where T = G/M . For
i ∈ I, let y1i , ..., yni be the projections of the free generators x1 , . . . , xn of Fn in the factor Gi , and
z1i , ..., zni be their natural images in the quotients Gi /Mi . We call two indices i and j equivalent if
the n-tuples (z1i , ..., zni ) and (z1j , ..., znj ) are equal (if we identify both Ti and Tj with T ). So the
set I is a disjoint union of at most |T |n equivalence classes.
      For an equivalence class J, we denote by HJ the projection of H to the direct power GJ .
It follows from the definition of the equivalence that the projections of the n-tuple of the free
generators of Fn to Gj are equal modulo M J for all j ∈ J, whence the image of Fn in GJ /M J
is contained in the diagonal of (G/M )J and the quotient R = HJ /M J has order at most |T |.
Moreover, the abelian normal subgroups Mj of HJ are isomorphic R-modules for all j ∈ J.
                                                                                                 log |T |
      By Lemma 4, the order of the projection SJ of Fn to HJ does not exceed |G||G| 2 |M |n|M | .
Since the number of equivalence classes J is at most |T |n , and the group Fn is contained in the
direct product of subgroups HJ over all J, we have
                                                        log2 |T |                 n
                                      |Fn | ≤ (|G||G|               |M |n|M | )|T | .

The logarithm of the right-hand side is bounded from above by cn|T |n , where the constant c does
not depend on n. It follows that pot G ≤ |T |, as required.

    The statement of Theorem 1 follows from the following
    Proposition 2. (Gap for the values of pot G). Let G be a non-trivial finite group. Then
pot G = |G| if G is a monolithic group whose monolith is non-abelian. Otherwise pot G ≤ d < |G|
for some divisor d of |G|.

Proof. The first statement of the proposition is proved in Section 2, the second one follows from
Lemma 3 and Proposition 1.


4    Proof of Theorem 2
Note that a finite prime ring A cannot contain two different minimal ideals, and multiplication
is nonzero on the unique minimal ideal. If, for brevity, rings with zero multiplication are called
abelian (as in Lie theory), A is a monolithic ring with a non-abelian monolith M .
                                                                                                      5


    Such a reformulation makes Theorem 2 very similar to Theorem 1, and the proofs are similar
as well. Of course, the variety var A contains rings, not groups; one works with subrings instead of
subgroups and with ideals instead of normal subgroups. If the expression ’centralize each other’ is
replaced by ’annihilate each other on both sides’ in the proof of Lemma 1, we obtain the formulation
and proof of an analogous Lemma 1’ for rings.
    The obvious changes in vocabulary are also sufficient for the formulation and proof of a Lemma
2’ analogous to Lemma 2. (Of course, one refers to Lemma 1’ instead of Lemma 1 in the proof.)
The last paragraph of Section 2 can be trivially reformulated as well. The same changes lead to
the formulation and proof of Lemma 3.
    Let R be a ring, and N be an abelian ideal of R. Then for a ∈ N and r ∈ R, the products
ra and ar depend only on the coset r + N , and so the left and right multiplications of a by the
elements of R/N are well defined. Given two abelian ideals M and M ′ in R, we say that these
ideals are similar in R if there is an isomorphism of their additive groups α : M → M ′ such that
α(rm) = rα(m) and α(mr) = α(m)r for any m ∈ M and r ∈ R. Clearly, the similarity of ideals is
an equivalence relation.

    Lemma 4’. Let R be a ring, and let N be an ideal of R that is a direct sum ⊕i Mi of finite
abelian ideals Mi of cardinality m that are similar in R. Then any n elements of N are contained
in an ideal L of R of cardinality at most mnm .

   The proof follows that of Lemma 4, where αij is an R-similarity of the ideals Mi and Mj , and
the minimal ideals containing a ∈ Mi and the ’diagonal’ element b (as there) are similar in R.

    Lemma 5’. Let A be a finite ring and N an abelian ideal of a ring H ∈ var A, N = ⊕i Mi be
a direct sum of similar in H ideals Mi of cardinality m, and R = H/N . Then for every n ≥ 1, any
                                                          log |R|
n-generated subring S of H has cardinality at most |A||A| 2 mnm .

    For the proof of Lemma 5’, one changes the vocabulary (in particular, the words ’isomorphic
modules’ are replaced by ’ideals similar in G’). In the proof, the element yi (i > k) is obtained as a
sum of xi and an element from the subring K generated by x1 , . . . , xk . Now L is the minimal ideal
of S containing yk+1 , . . . , yn , and S = K + L.
    Only obvious changes are needed in the formulations and proofs of Propositions 1’ and 2’. This
completes the proof of Theorem 2. The author believes that similar modifications would lead to
the proof of an analogue of Theorem 2 for Ω-rings.

     Remark 2. Let A be a finite-dimensional (non-associative) algebra over a finite field k, and
let Fn denote the n-generated free algebra in the variety var A of algebras over k generated by A.
Then one can formulate an analogue of Theorem 2 and prove it without any new assumptions. In
this setting, however, it is preferable to consider the dimension function d(n) = dimk Fn , which
                                                                                                p     is
                                                                                                 n
the logarithm of the cardinality function |Fn |. Thus the potential pot A of A is lim supn→∞ d(n),
and Theorem 2 is modified as follows:
     Let A be a finite-dimensional (nonassociative) algebra over a finite field k. The equality pot A =
|A| holds if and only if A is a prime algebra.
     Moreover, if A is a prime algebra, then there exist positive constants c1 and c2 such that
c1 |A|n < dimk Fn < c2 |A|n for the n-generated free algebras Fn in the variety var A.
6                                             A.Yu. Olshanskii


5    Examples and questions
It is worth finding potentials for various classes of finite groups and rings. By Theorem 1 and
Lemma 3, it suffices to examine monolithic groups and rings having an abelian monolith.
    Example 1. Let G be a finite dihedral group. If it is a 2-group, then pot G = 1, because G
is nilpotent. Otherwise pot G ≥ 2 as mentioned in the Introduction. On the other hand, G has an
abelian subgroup of index 2, and therefore pot G = 2 in this case by Proposition 1.
    Example 2. Let G be a Miller–Moreno group, that is a non-abelian finite group, all of whose
proper subgroups are abelian. We assume that G is not nilpotent, since otherwise pot G = 1. Then,
for two distinct prime numbers p and q, G = P Q, where P is an elementary abelian p-group, Q
is a cyclic q-group, and Qq lies in the center of G (see [8], 9.1.9). So any non-abelian monolithic
quotient Ḡ of G belongs to the variety V consisting of groups having a normal elementary abelian
p-subgroup with an elementary abelian q-group as a quotient. Then Ḡ generates the variety V
                                                                             n
(see [7], 54.41). The order of the free group Fn in V is equal to q n p(n−1)q +1 ([7], 21.13), whence
pot G = pot Ḡ = q. For example, pot A4 = 3 for the alternating group A4 of degree 4.
    Example 3. The following product of varieties of associative algebras (no 1 in the signa-
ture) over a field was introduced in the paper of G. Bergman and J. Lewin [2]. The product
UV of two varieties is defined by the set of all identities u(x1 , . . . , xk )v(xk+1 , . . . xk+ℓ ) = 0, where
u(x1 , . . . , xk ) = 0 is an identity of the variety U and v(x1 , . . . xℓ ) = 0 is an identity of V. Assume
that U = var A and V = var B, where A and B are non-zero finite associative algebras over a
finite field k. Then, by Proposition 18 and Theorem 20 of [1], the variety UV is generated by a
finite algebra C over k such that pot C = (pot A)(pot B).
    Example 4. Given a finite field k, there is only one non-abelian 2-dimensional Lie algebra L
over k up to isomorphism. It has basis (e, f ) such that ef = −f e = f and e2 = f 2 = 0. There is a
1-dimensional monolith ⟨f ⟩, and pot L ≤ |L/⟨f ⟩| = |k| by Proposition 1’. To obtain the opposite
inequality, we construct an n-generated algebra A in var L as follows.
    Consider the set V ∗ of |k|n−1 linear functions α : V → k, where V is an n − 1-dimensional
abelian Lie algebra over k. For each α ∈ V ∗ , let ⟨fα ⟩ be a 1-dimensional Lie algebra and define
the Lie module Mα = ⟨fα ⟩ over V by the rule vfα = α(v)fα for v ∈ V . These rules define the
semidirect
P           sum A of V and the ideal I = ⊕α∈V ∗ Mα . The ideal I is generated by one element
   α fα since the weights α are pairwise distinct. So A is an n-generated Lie algebra of dimension
n + |k|n−1 . It is embedded in a direct power of L whence A ∈ var L. (For each α, consider a
homomorphism
          p      that sends v to α(v)e, sends fα to f , and kills the other weight spaces.) Since
limn→∞ n + |k|n−1 = |k|, we have pot L ≥ |k|.
          n


    Question 1. Is the potential pot G an integer for every finite group G?
                                p
    Question 2. Does limn→∞ n log |Fn | exist for any finite group G, where Fn are the n-generated
free groups in the variety var G?
                                                              |Fn+1 |
   Question 3. In the notation of Question 2, does limn→∞ log
                                                            log |Fn | exist? (Then it is equal to
the limit from Question 2 and to pot G.)
    Similar questions for finite algebras have been formulated in [1].
    If a finite group G has a central subgroup Z and the quotient G/Z is simple (in particular,
if G is quasisimple), then pot G = pot (G/Z) by Theorem 1 and Proposition 1. The equality
pot G = pot (G/Z) = 1 also holds if G/Z is a non-trivial nilpotent group. So I venture to ask
                                                                                                   7


    Question 4. Let Z be a proper subgroup (subring) of a finite group (ring) G that centralizes
(resp., annihilates) G. Does the equality pot G = pot (G/Z) hold?
    If a group G has an abelian normal subgroup N and Q = G/N , there is a semidirect product
Ḡ = QN , Q ∩ N = {1}, such that the action by conjugation of Q on N coincides in G and in Ḡ.
The following construction (depending on N ) shows that Ḡ = Ḡ(N ) belongs to var G.
    Let H be the direct product G1 × G2 of two copies of G and D be the diagonal of G. By
definition, K = DN1 = DN2 , where N1 and N2 are copies of N . Note that D ∩ N1 = D ∩ N2 = {1}
and L = D ∩ (N1 × N2 ) is the diagonal of N1 × N2 . It is a normal subgroup of K since N is abelian.
Denote the quotient K/L by Ḡ. Then the image Q of D in K/L = Ḡ has trivial intersection with
the image of N1 (= image of N2 ) in Ḡ, and Ḡ is the required semidirect product.
    The same construction defines the semidirect sum Ḡ ∈ var G if G is a ring and N is an abelian
ideal of G. This leads to the following generalization of Question 4.
   Question 5. Let N be an abelian normal subgroup (ideal) in a finite group (resp., ring) G. In
the above notation, does the equality pot G = pot (Ḡ) hold?
